summary: Describes how a host can detect DNS64 and learn the IPv6 prefix used for address synthesis, using the well-known name ipv4only.arpa. Learning this lets nodes synthesize addresses locally and possibly avoid NAT64 on dual-stack and multi-interface deployments.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7050 defines a DNS query that lets a host discover the IPv6 prefix used by a NAT64 network. The host looks for two known IPv4 addresses inside the synthesized IPv6 answers.

questions: how to discover the nat64 prefix
how does a host detect dns64
subtitle: Discover the IPv6 prefix used to synthesize addresses for IPv4 destinations on a NAT64 network.

tldr.problem: An IPv6-only host may need to create an IPv6 address for an IPv4 destination itself, and it needs to know the network's translation prefix.
tldr.mechanism: The host queries AAAA records for ipv4only.arpa. and searches the synthesized addresses for 192.0.0.170 or 192.0.0.171.
tldr.outcome: A host can use the discovered prefix for local address synthesis and check whether DNS64 is present. RFC 7050 is updated by RFC 8880.

facts.label: Rediscovery time
facts.value: 10 seconds before synthetic record TTL expires

today: RFC 7050 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2013. The unit metadata says RFC 8880 updates it and lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a Host Needs the Prefix
sections.content:
DNS64 can synthesize an IPv6 address for an IPv4-only destination, but it cannot help applications that receive an IPv4 address directly instead of using DNS. A host running a validating DNSSEC resolver may also need to perform synthesis itself.

To synthesize an address locally, the host needs the translation prefix, called Pref64::/n. This RFC provides a best-effort discovery method; the address-synthesis procedure itself is outside its scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A host may need to make an IPv6 address for an IPv4 destination on its own. To do that, it first has to learn the prefix used by its NAT64 network.

sections.title: Discovering the Prefix with DNS
sections.content:
A node queries the AAAA records for ipv4only.arpa.. The query's Checking Disabled bit MUST be zero so a DNS64 server performs synthesis. A reply containing AAAA records indicates that the network is synthesizing addresses.

The node searches the returned IPv6 addresses for the well-known IPv4 addresses 192.0.0.170 and 192.0.0.171, at the locations permitted by RFC 6052. The part surrounding a match identifies a candidate prefix. If multiple prefixes are returned, the node uses all of them for local synthesis in the order received.

If discovery has no positive answer, the node may query A records for the same name. It caches discovery replies and SHOULD repeat the query ten seconds before a synthetic AAAA record's TTL expires.
sections.plainLanguage: The host asks for an IPv6 address for a name that has only known IPv4 addresses. It finds those IPv4 values inside the answer to determine which prefix the network added.

sections.title: Checking Who Supplied the Prefix
sections.content:
An attacker who can alter DNS replies could influence the discovered prefix. This could redirect traffic, prevent a connection, or let an attacker observe traffic. A node SHOULD use a trusted DNS64 server over a secure channel or use DNSSEC.

For DNSSEC validation, the node queries the discovered address's PTR record, checks whether the returned NAT64 domain is trusted, then checks the domain's AAAA record against the initial discovery answer and validates it. If no trusted domain matches, it MUST NOT continue the validation procedure. DNSSEC does not prove that the node is on the network where the prefix should be used, and it cannot validate the Well-Known Prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: A fake DNS answer can lead the host to use a harmful prefix. DNSSEC can check that signed records match a trusted domain, but it cannot prove that the host is on the intended network.

sections.title: Testing Whether the Prefix Works
sections.content:
After discovery, a node SHOULD check that the prefix reaches a working NAT64 and an IPv4 destination. It may use an implementation-specific test server or try an actual connection. The RFC also describes how an operator can provide an ICMPv6 Echo responder for this purpose.

With that method, the node sends an Echo Request through the discovered prefix and retries after one second and two seconds if no reply arrives. It MUST NOT send a connectivity check to an address returned by the ipv4only.arpa. query, because no server is operated at that address and the check could leak to the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding a prefix does not prove it works. A host can test it with an operator-provided server, but it must not test the special discovery address itself.

sections.title: DNS and Operator Behavior
sections.content:
The authoritative server for ipv4only.arpa. SHALL set a record TTL of at least 60 minutes, and the zone MUST be signed with DNSSEC. DNS64 operators control how many synthesized AAAA records they return.

Returning multiple records can give a node multiple prefixes, but does not guarantee which prefix it will use. Returning a single synthetic record is the only guaranteed method described for steering a node to one prefix or rotating the prefix through its TTL.
sections.plainLanguage: The discovery name has a minimum TTL and its DNS zone must be signed. Operators can influence which prefixes hosts learn by choosing how many synthetic records to return.

sections.title: Limits and Exit Strategy
sections.content:
If an attacker changes the prefix, traffic may go to an unintended destination. The RFC describes denial of service, flooding, and eavesdropping as possible results. A node should use trusted DNS and validation where available.

The method does not discover rules that map different IPv4 ranges to different prefixes, so a node uses the discovered prefix for any locally synthesized IPv4 address. The RFC calls this a transition tool and says a node SHOULD provide a configuration option to disable discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Prefix discovery cannot protect every network configuration or remove the risks of address translation. The RFC describes it as a transition tool and recommends an option to turn it off.
